newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand's Chavalit silent after meeting with king.
newsitem.headline: Thailand's Chavalit silent after meeting with king.

text.p: Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh and Thailand's two top financial officials made no comment on Thursday evening after spending more than 2-1/2 hours with King Bhumibol Adulyadej.

Chavalit refused to speak to reporters after leaving the palace and Finance Minster Thanong Bidaya only said that it was not correct to make any comments after such a meeting. Central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi was also at the meeting.

"There was nothing special in the audience with the King," government spokesman Warathep Ratanakorn said. "The prime minister just briefed His Majesty on the economic situation and the measures to resolve it."

Although he is a constitutional monarch seen as above politics, King Bhumibol's influence over policy is critical. In the past he has intervened in times of turmoil to halt violence and prevent further unrest. His word is always heeded.
The government on Tuesday announced a series of tough austerity measures aimed at boosting the nation's economy, which has hit its slowest rate of growth in more than a decade.
The measures, imposed after receiving recommendations from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), included the shock suspension of more than half the country's finance companies.
Other measures included tough monetary and fiscal measures like an unpopular three percent rise in the value added tax, a cap on inflation and a cut in the current account deficit.
The meeting with the king took place as rumours swirled throughout Bangkok and financial markets that a major decision may be taken during the talks and that it could involve a change of government.

The Thai stock market, which has fallen sharply over the past two trading days, was boosted by news of the meeting and finished on a positive note. The baht also firmed against the dollar as currency traders expected some positive news.
Ever since the government announced the austerity measures on Tuesday, rumours of a possible coup, massive protests or a change of government have spread in Bangkok.
Chavalit and the military have repeatedly dismissed the prospect of using military force to solve the economic crisis.
The rumours were partly due to uncertainty over the fate of the remaining finance companies and questions over the ability of the government to handle the fragile economy.
Earlier in the day Chavalit held a meeting of his New Aspiration Party (NAP) to warn them of the consequences of speaking about the fragile economy.

"The prime minister has warned party members who have nothing to do with economic issues not to talk too much about the issue because it would lead to public confusion," a NAP member said after the meeting.
Chavalit also requested radio and television stations tone down reports of political and economic rumours.

Bhokin Bhalakula, minister of the prime minister's office, said he conveyed the message to the stations and said he did not demand one-sided stories but only asked them to carry accurate information so the public could form its own opinions.
An army spokesman, who denied that a coup was in the offing, said the King's decision to grant an audience with Chavalit was a positive sign for the government.
